findings.original_claim: Stewart, R. Jamie, Scott, Vivian, Haszeldine, R. Stuart (University of Edinburgh), Ainger, Dominic & Argent, Steve (Arup) (2014). findings.interpretation: The study’s core insight — that CCS at scale in Europe requires transboundary transport and offshore storage — has been absorbed into EU policy, but the envisaged integrated pipeline network has been delayed by roughly a decade and reshaped into clusters linked by shipping, with 2030 ambitions at the low end of the 2014 scenarios. findings.original_claim: Keaver, Laura, Webber, Laura, Dee, Anne, Shiely, Frances, Marsh, Tim, Balanda, Kevin P. & Perry, Ivan J. (2013). findings.interpretation: Partly along the envisioned pathway — adult obesity in Ireland is high and still rising — but much more slowly than the extrapolation implied. findings.title: Immigration and integration scenarios for Europe to 2050 (2013)
findings.original_claim: Avramov, Dragana (2013). Immigration and integration scenarios in global Europe: Forward-looking up to 2050. Sociologija 55(2), 169–186. Population and Social Policy Consultants, Brussels. https://doi.org/10.2298/SOC1302169A (diamond open access; the full text could not be opened during this review, so the abstract was used).
findings.interpretation: The methodological recommendation developed broadly along the envisioned pathway: integration and labour-market scenarios became standard companions of EU population projections. The migration pathway itself was transformed by unexpected events — an asylum surge, a pandemic and a war — rather than shaped by planned recruitment, and the zero-immigration storyline survives as a counterfactual reference case in official projections. The 2050 horizon has not been reached.

findings.review_status_detail: Abstract-only assessment. The original was read as an abstract; the Eurostat datasets and the two JRC reports were opened directly.
findings.full_review_original_claim: Paraphrase from the abstract: the article compares EU population prospects to 2050 under several migration hypotheses — business as usual, replacement migration, and recruitment to fill gaps in labour supply — and builds a deliberate shock storyline of no immigration into the EU, setting out the social consequences of the zero immigration that, according to the abstract, some policy circles desired. Its closing recommendation is that assessments of future immigration needs should combine integration scenarios with demographic projections and labour-market needs. Key phrase (abstract): “No immigration into European Union” as a shock hypothesis. The catalogued excerpt (HISTORICAL-CLAIMS record 448) reproduces only the recommendation sentence, which is methodological; the substantive future content lies in the comparison of migration hypotheses and the zero-immigration warning.
